rows.context: The following figure shows a circuit diagram. We can find the currents through and potential differences across different resistors using Kirchhoff's rules.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same drawing as Q34 (a); see that row's note. The arm 'bg' is identified only by the labels in the figure, and the component values needed to compute the current appear nowhere in the passage. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
The arm bg is the middle branch of the network, the one containing \(\mathrm{R_1} = 10\ \Omega\).
The middle branch and the right-hand branch are both connected between the same two nodes -- the top wire and the bottom wire -- so they are in PARALLEL. The right-hand branch has \(\mathrm{R_2}\) and \(\mathrm{R_3}\) in series, giving \(5 + 5 = 10\ \Omega\), so the two parallel branches happen to have equal resistance:
\(R_p = \dfrac{10\times 10}{10 + 10} = 5\ \Omega\).
This combination is in series with the internal resistance of the cell, so the total resistance of the circuit is \(5 + 1 = 6\ \Omega\), and the current drawn from the cell is
\(\mathrm{I_1} = \dfrac{E}{R_p + r} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}0}{6} = 1\ \mathrm{A}\).
Since the two parallel branches have EQUAL resistance, this current divides equally between them. The current through the arm bg is therefore
\(\mathrm{I_2} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{A}\).
The same result follows from Kirchhoff's loop rule, which is the method the question's own passage points to. Taking the loop abgha,
\(-6 + 10\,\mathrm{I_2} + \mathrm{I_1} = 0\), so \(\mathrm{I_1} + 10\,\mathrm{I_2} = 6\)  ... (1)
and taking the loop acfha, in which the right-hand branch carries \(\mathrm{I_1} - \mathrm{I_2}\),
\(-6 + 10\left(\mathrm{I_1} - \mathrm{I_2}\right) + \mathrm{I_1} = 0\), so \(11\,\mathrm{I_1} - 10\,\mathrm{I_2} = 6\)  ... (2)
Adding (1) and (2) eliminates \(\mathrm{I_2}\) and gives \(12\,\mathrm{I_1} = 12\), so \(\mathrm{I_1} = 1\) A, and then (1) gives \(\mathrm{I_2} = 0{\cdot}5\) A.

rows.stem: Find the potential difference across resistance \(\mathrm{R_3}\).
rows.context: The following figure shows a circuit diagram. We can find the currents through and potential differences across different resistors using Kirchhoff's rules.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same drawing as Q34 (a); see that row's note. \(\mathrm{R_3}\) is named only in the figure and its value appears nowhere in the passage. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{R_3}\) lies in the right-hand branch, so the first step is to find the current in that branch.
The middle branch carries \(\mathrm{R_1} = 10\ \Omega\) and the right-hand branch carries \(\mathrm{R_2}\) and \(\mathrm{R_3}\) in series, \(5 + 5 = 10\ \Omega\). The two are connected between the same pair of nodes, so they are in parallel:
\(R_p = \dfrac{10\times10}{10+10} = 5\ \Omega\).
Adding the internal resistance of the cell in series gives a total of \(5 + 1 = 6\ \Omega\), so the current supplied by the cell is
\(\mathrm{I_1} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}0}{6} = 1\ \mathrm{A}\).
The two parallel branches have equal resistance, so this splits equally and the current down the right-hand branch is
\(\mathrm{I_1} - \mathrm{I_2} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{A}\).
Because \(\mathrm{R_2}\) and \(\mathrm{R_3}\) are in SERIES, the whole of that current passes through \(\mathrm{R_3}\). By Ohm's law,
\(V_{\mathrm{R_3}} = \left(\mathrm{I_1} - \mathrm{I_2}\right)\times\mathrm{R_3} = 0{\cdot}5\times 5 = 2{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{V}\).
The potential difference across \(\mathrm{R_3}\) is \(2{\cdot}5\) V.
As a check on the whole calculation: \(\mathrm{R_2}\) carries the same current and so also drops \(2{\cdot}5\) V, the two together accounting for the \(5{\cdot}0\) V across the parallel combination, and the remaining \(1{\cdot}0\) V is dropped across the internal resistance -- which adds up to the \(6{\cdot}0\) V emf of the cell.

rows.stem: What is the power dissipated in resistance \(\mathrm{R_2}\) ?
rows.context: The following figure shows a circuit diagram. We can find the currents through and potential differences across different resistors using Kirchhoff's rules.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same drawing as Q34 (a); see that row's note. \(\mathrm{R_2}\) is named only in the figure and its value appears nowhere in the passage. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{R_2}\) lies in the right-hand branch, so the first step is to find the current in that branch.
The middle branch carries \(\mathrm{R_1} = 10\ \Omega\) and the right-hand branch carries \(\mathrm{R_2}\) and \(\mathrm{R_3}\) in series, \(5 + 5 = 10\ \Omega\). The two are connected between the same pair of nodes, so they are in parallel:
\(R_p = \dfrac{10\times10}{10+10} = 5\ \Omega\).
Adding the internal resistance of the cell in series gives a total of \(5 + 1 = 6\ \Omega\), so the current supplied by the cell is
\(\mathrm{I_1} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}0}{6} = 1\ \mathrm{A}\),
and since the two parallel branches have equal resistance this divides equally. The current through \(\mathrm{R_2}\) is therefore
\(\mathrm{I_1} - \mathrm{I_2} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{A}\).
The power dissipated in a resistor carrying a current I is \(P = I^{2}R\), so
\(P = \left(\mathrm{I_1} - \mathrm{I_2}\right)^{2}\times\mathrm{R_2} = \left(0{\cdot}5\right)^{2}\times 5 = 0{\cdot}25\times 5\),
\(P = 1{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{W}\).
The power dissipated in \(\mathrm{R_2}\) is \(1{\cdot}25\) W. Using \(P = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}\) with the \(2{\cdot}5\) V across it, or \(P = VI = 2{\cdot}5\times0{\cdot}5\), gives the same figure.

rows.stem: Trace the path of the ray showing its passage through the prism.
rows.context: Strontium titanate is a rare oxide — a natural mineral found in Siberia. It is used as a substitute for diamond because its refractive index and critical angle are \(2{\cdot}41\) and \(24{\cdot}5°\), respectively, which are approximately equal to the refractive index and critical angle of diamond. It has all the properties of diamond. Even an expert jeweller is unable to differentiate between diamond and strontium titanate. A ray of light is incident normally on one face of an equilateral triangular prism ABC made of strontium titanate.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the answer to this sub-part IS a traced path through the drawn prism, and the passage does not say which face the ray strikes. Described: an upward-pointing triangle with its vertices labelled A (apex), B (bottom left) and C (bottom right), the apex angle annotated 60°, and an arrow drawn outside the triangle approaching one of its faces. Withheld: which face the incoming arrow meets, which is what fixes where the ray then strikes the second surface. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
The ray falls on the face AB at right angles, so it enters the prism WITHOUT bending: at normal incidence both the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction are zero. It therefore travels straight across the prism and meets the second face AC.
The geometry fixes the angle of incidence there. The ray inside the prism is perpendicular to AB, and the prism is equilateral so that each of its angles is \(60^{\circ}\); the normal to AC therefore makes an angle of \(60^{\circ}\) with the ray. Hence the ray strikes AC at an angle of incidence
\(i = 60^{\circ}\).
Now compare this with the critical angle. The passage gives \(i_c = 24{\cdot}5^{\circ}\) for strontium titanate, and
\(60^{\circ} > 24{\cdot}5^{\circ}\),
so the light cannot pass out through AC. It undergoes TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION at that face, the angle of reflection being \(60^{\circ}\) as well.
The reflected ray then travels down through the prism and meets the third face BC along ITS normal, so it emerges through BC without any further bending.
Path to be traced, therefore: in through AB undeviated, total internal reflection at AC, and out through BC perpendicular to it -- the ray having been turned through \(90^{\circ}\) altogether.

rows.stem: Find the velocity of light through the prism.
rows.context: Strontium titanate is a rare oxide — a natural mineral found in Siberia. It is used as a substitute for diamond because its refractive index and critical angle are \(2{\cdot}41\) and \(24{\cdot}5°\), respectively, which are approximately equal to the refractive index and critical angle of diamond. It has all the properties of diamond. Even an expert jeweller is unable to differentiate between diamond and strontium titanate. A ray of light is incident normally on one face of an equilateral triangular prism ABC made of strontium titanate.
rows.solution:
The refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium:
\(n = \dfrac{c}{v}\), so \(v = \dfrac{c}{n}\).
The passage gives the refractive index of strontium titanate as \(2{\cdot}41\), and \(c = 3\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Hence
\(v = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{2{\cdot}41} = 1{\cdot}24\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Light travels through the prism at about \(1{\cdot}24\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), roughly two-fifths of its speed in vacuum. It is this large slowing down, and the small critical angle that goes with it, that makes the material behave optically like diamond.

rows.stem: Briefly explain two applications of total internal reflection.
rows.context: Strontium titanate is a rare oxide — a natural mineral found in Siberia. It is used as a substitute for diamond because its refractive index and critical angle are \(2{\cdot}41\) and \(24{\cdot}5°\), respectively, which are approximately equal to the refractive index and critical angle of diamond. It has all the properties of diamond. Even an expert jeweller is unable to differentiate between diamond and strontium titanate. A ray of light is incident normally on one face of an equilateral triangular prism ABC made of strontium titanate.
rows.solution:
Any two of the following applications, briefly explained.
1. OPTICAL FIBRE. An optical fibre is a very fine thread with a core of higher refractive index surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index. Light entering one end strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle for that pair of media, so it is totally internally reflected instead of escaping. Repeating this thousands of times over, it is guided along the fibre, following even its bends, and emerges at the far end with very little loss of intensity. Optical fibres carry telephone and internet signals over long distances and are used in the endoscope, which lets a doctor see inside the body.
2. BRILLIANCE OF DIAMOND. Diamond has a very high refractive index, about \(2{\cdot}42\), and therefore a very small critical angle, about \(24^{\circ}\). Light entering a cut stone meets face after face at angles exceeding this, so it is totally internally reflected many times within the stone before finally escaping from a few faces only. The light is thus concentrated into a few directions, which is what makes a diamond sparkle. The strontium titanate of the passage is used as a substitute precisely because its refractive index and critical angle are almost the same.
3. MIRAGE. On a hot day the layer of air just above a road is much hotter, and therefore optically rarer, than the air above it. A ray of light travelling downwards from the sky passes from denser to rarer layers and is refracted away from the normal at each, bending more and more until it strikes a layer at more than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected. It then curves upwards to the observer's eye, which sees the sky as though reflected in a sheet of water lying on the road.
4. TOTALLY REFLECTING PRISMS. A right-angled isosceles glass prism turns a beam of light through \(90^{\circ}\) or through \(180^{\circ}\), or inverts an image, by total internal reflection at its hypotenuse face, the angle of incidence there being \(45^{\circ}\), which exceeds the critical angle for glass. Such prisms are used in periscopes, binoculars and cameras in place of mirrors, because no light at all is lost.

rows.stem: Define total internal reflection of light. Give two conditions for it.
rows.context: Strontium titanate is a rare oxide — a natural mineral found in Siberia. It is used as a substitute for diamond because its refractive index and critical angle are \(2{\cdot}41\) and \(24{\cdot}5°\), respectively, which are approximately equal to the refractive index and critical angle of diamond. It has all the properties of diamond. Even an expert jeweller is unable to differentiate between diamond and strontium titanate. A ray of light is incident normally on one face of an equilateral triangular prism ABC made of strontium titanate.
rows.solution:
DEFINITION. When light travelling in an optically DENSER medium reaches the boundary with an optically RARER medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle for that pair of media, no light at all is refracted into the rarer medium; the whole of it is turned back into the denser medium at the boundary. This phenomenon is called TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION. It is total in a sense that ordinary reflection is not: at an ordinary reflecting surface some of the energy is always transmitted or absorbed, whereas here the reflected beam carries practically the whole of the incident energy.
TWO CONDITIONS FOR IT TO OCCUR:
1. The light must be travelling FROM an optically denser medium TOWARDS an optically rarer one, that is from the medium of higher refractive index to the medium of lower refractive index.
2. The angle of incidence at the interface must be GREATER than the critical angle for that pair of media. The critical angle \(i_c\) is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium becomes \(90^{\circ}\), and it is given by
\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{n_{\text{rarer}}}{n_{\text{denser}}}\).
